content: There were moderate concerns regarding the relevance of the data, as only two studies were included, both originating from high-income countries. The adequacy of the data was also a point of moderate concern, although the data from these studies were relatively robust. The guideline on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services emphasized the avoidance of feeding bottles and teats. Out of 630 studies assessed for inclusion, only three were deemed eligible. These studies explored mothers' values and preferences regarding the avoidance of artificial teats and bottles (conducted in Australia, Sweden, and the United Kingdom) and the use of cup feeding (conducted in Australia and the United Kingdom). Mothers of normal-term infants and those with infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) expressed that using a bottle was easy and convenient. They felt no need for training, as the skill seemed to come naturally. Bottles were often seen as the natural option when breastfeeding presented challenges. Among mothers of very preterm and very low-birth-weight infants, breastfeeding was considered the best choice. However, bottle feeding was also viewed as a viable alternative, particularly when mothers were emotionally drained after prolonged hospital stays or when dealing with infants with medical issues at home. The confidence in the evidence was low, but there were no methodological limitations or concerns about coherence. The findings were consistent across mothers of normal-term infants and those with preterm or very low-birth-weight infants. However, there were moderate concerns about the relevance of the data, as the studies were limited to high-income countries. The adequacy of the data was also a minor concern, though the data were relatively thick. Mothers found cup feeding to be difficult, describing it as messy, time-consuming, and wasteful due to spills. Infants were often not satisfied with cup feeding. In trials where mothers were assigned to cup feed, the majority eventually introduced bottles. The findings were consistent across mothers of normal-term and preterm infants. However, there were moderate concerns about the relevance and adequacy of the data, as only two studies were included, both from high-income countries. Regarding breastfeeding policies in facilities providing maternity and newborn services, no studies were found that addressed maternal values and preferences. Similarly, no studies were identified on maternal values and preferences related to the training of health workers. In the context of antenatal breastfeeding education, 286 studies were assessed, and 18 were deemed eligible. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, Sweden, Uganda, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The findings were divided into two themes: the content and the method of antenatal breastfeeding education. Some mothers felt that infant feeding was not adequately discussed during the antenatal period. They desired more information from prenatal classes and formal institutional support for infant feeding. Many mothers, including those in Uganda and adolescent mothers, felt that antenatal education on feeding was insufficient or infrequent. Some mothers criticized the content of antenatal education for being overly biased toward breastfeeding, with insufficient discussion of other options or the challenges of breastfeeding. Practical information was preferred by mothers. The confidence in the evidence was moderate, with no concerns about methodological limitations or data adequacy. Most studies were of good quality and provided thick data. However, there were minor concerns about relevance, as only one study was from a low-income country, and none were from Asia or the Middle East. Mothers valued linkage to breastfeeding support after discharge. Regardless of the type of support (e.g., telephone, baby cafés, hospital visits, home visits, videoconferencing, or a combination of mechanisms), mothers appreciated having access to support after discharge. This support provided a greater sense of security, especially during the first postnatal week. The confidence in the evidence was moderate, with minor methodological limitations and no concerns about coherence. However, there were moderate concerns about relevance and adequacy, as most studies focused on maternal satisfaction with relatively thin data. A systematic review of health-care workers' values and preferences regarding breastfeeding support, as related to the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding and the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative, was conducted. The review included 62 eligible articles, with data extracted and organized by breastfeeding interventions. The GRADE-CERQual approach was used to assess the confidence in the findings, based on methodological limitations, relevance, coherence, and adequacy of data. Health workers valued and had favorable views toward early skin-to-skin contact after delivery. The benefits of skin-to-skin care were well-known and accepted among health-care personnel. Some providers considered skin-to-skin contact a way to improve efficiency while enhancing patient outcomes. However, there were minor concerns about methodological limitations and coherence, moderate concerns about relevance, and moderate concerns about data adequacy, as the data were relatively thin. Health workers expressed safety concerns about early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding during deliveries involving anesthesia, such as cesarean sections or epidural anesthesia. While maternity staff generally supported early skin-to-skin contact, they believed that initiating breastfeeding within 30 minutes of birth was not always feasible. Some studies reported that maternity staff found skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding in the operating room impractical and unsafe, particularly during complicated or cesarean deliveries. Barriers included hospital culture and staff preferences for quickly moving mothers and babies out of the delivery room. There were minor concerns about coherence, substantial concerns about relevance, and minor concerns about data adequacy, as most studies provided thick data from interviews and focus group discussions. Health workers in NICUs also had safety concerns about early breastfeeding and skin-to-skin contact when infants were admitted to intensive care.
